Why is everyone suddenly talking about Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility?

Because intelligence revealed in recent weeks indicates that the Islamic Republic may have moved thousands of uranium-enrichment centrifuges into tunnels deep inside the mountain. Israel also reportedly assesses that Iran transferred part of its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to the site for further work, possibly toward weapons-grade levels.

In other words, Iran may have moved both the machinery and the nuclear material needed to rebuild and advance its enrichment program into the most heavily fortified nuclear facility it has ever constructed.

That is why President Trump has now said that Pickaxe Mountain will be destroyed very soon.

The facility is believed to be buried more than 100 meters - approximately 330 feet - beneath solid rock. Its deepest chambers may therefore be beyond the reliable reach of America’s most powerful conventional bunker-buster, the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, also known as the MOP.

The GBU-57 weighs approximately 30,000 pounds and was designed to penetrate and destroy deeply buried, hardened targets. Repeated strikes could potentially collapse tunnel entrances, ventilation shafts, access routes, electrical systems, and other supporting infrastructure.

But disabling the facility from the outside and physically destroying its deepest underground chambers are two very different things.

This is why some analysts believe that the only weapon capable of destroying the heart of the facility may be a nuclear earth-penetrating weapon such as the B61-11, a variable-yield nuclear gravity bomb designed for hardened underground targets.

However, no one outside classified military circles can say with certainty whether such a weapon would completely destroy Pickaxe Mountain. Nor can anyone honestly guarantee minimal fallout. A nuclear ground or subsurface detonation would carry grave radiological, military, and geopolitical consequences.

Other options may include repeated GBU-57 strikes, collapsing every entrance and ventilation shaft, destroying the surrounding infrastructure, sabotage, or a ground operation. Those methods might render the facility unusable without necessarily pulverizing every chamber beneath the mountain.

One thing is crystal clear: the Islamic Republic did not bury thousands of centrifuges and possibly highly enriched uranium beneath hundreds of feet of rock because its nuclear program is peaceful.

They built this nuclear fortress to survive.

Trump says it will be destroyed very soon.

The world may soon discover whether even Pickaxe Mountain is beyond America’s reach.

🌍 Stablecoins are becoming more than a faster payment rail.

A new BIS paper examined stablecoin flows and traditional dollarisation across more than 130 economies.

The researchers found that both tend to grow under similar conditions: currency pressure, banking stress and sovereign crises.

Both can also become difficult to reverse once established.

The key difference is access.

Traditional dollar deposits move through the banking system. Stablecoins can provide access to dollar liquidity outside much of that infrastructure and appear less affected by capital-flow restrictions.

That changes how the asset should be understood.

A stablecoin is not only a place to wait between trades.

It can also be:

• a payment rail
• a store of dollar value
• an alternative to local banking infrastructure
• a channel through which capital crosses borders

The price may remain close to $1.

The wider risk still depends on the issuer, reserves, liquidity, jurisdiction and the system surrounding the token.

The token may be stable.
Its role in the financial system is not simple.

🔗 Source: BIS Working Paper No. 1370, July 21, 2026
